Today, we’re donating
Agent Skills
, the open standard that gives AI agents specialized knowledge and workflows, to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF). More than 70 agent platforms, including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and VS Code, have integrated Agent Skills since we published the standard in December 2025.
Agent interoperability through simplicity
A skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file that teaches an agent a specific task or domain, along with any scripts or reference material it needs. We developed skills while working on Claude Code. It handled general knowledge work well, but often lacked the procedural knowledge that real business tasks need. Within weeks of our October 2025 launch, developers published thousands of skills on GitHub and wrote loaders for Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode. We then published Agent Skills as an open standard, under its own GitHub organization and domain, so any agent could use it. So far, 1 million skills have been published and nearly 280 million installed.
Donating Agent Skills to AAIF
We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral. Today, we are donating the standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation,
which we co-founded
with Block and OpenAI last year, and to which we donated the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The AAIF will provide a neutral home to the standard going forward, ensuring the community has a say in where Agent Skills go next.
We are donating the Agent Skills name and logo, the GitHub organization, and the
agentskills.io
domain. You can continue to use the standard or contribute to it without joining the AAIF.
Engineers from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and other companies will maintain the standard as individuals, with David Soria Parra and Mahesh Murag as Lead Maintainers.
What comes next
We’ve proposed starting with a roadmap covering versioned releases, a formal proposal process, and security guidance for people who write and install skills. As with MCP, the project will continue to prioritize community input and transparent decision-making. You can join the project’s
Discord
to give feedback on proposed specification changes.
Thank you to the developers who built with Agent Skills from the start, and to the teams who brought skills into their products. Read the specification at
agentskills.io
and join the discussion on
GitHub
.

Monthly API credits for Max and Team plans
Updated over a week ago
Copy for LLM
Max and Team plans include monthly credits for the Claude Platform. Use them to build Claude into your own apps and agents with the Claude API. This article explains who's eligible, how to claim your credit, what it covers, and what happens when it runs out.
Available on Max and Team plans, including discounted Team plans. Free, Pro, and Enterprise plans aren't eligible.
Monthly credits by plan
Plan
Monthly credit
Max 5x
$100
Max 20x
$200
Team (Standard seats)
$20 per seat*
Team (Premium seats)
$100 per seat*
Discounted Team plans (Nonprofit, Scientists)
$20 USD per Standard seat and $100 USD per Premium seat*
*On Team plans, credits for all seats are pooled into one monthly balance, capped at $500. For example, a team with three Standard seats and two Premium seats receives $260 a month. The pool is calculated from the seats on the plan when the credits are granted.
Eligibility
Active plan.
Your Max or Team subscription must be active and in good standing.
Seven days on the plan.
New subscribers can claim once they've been on an eligible plan for seven days.
Mobile subscriptions.
You can subscribe on the web, iOS, or Android. Claim your credits on claude.ai in a web browser.
No payment method needed.
You don't need to add a card on Claude Platform to claim or use the credit.
How to claim your credit
To claim your credit, you link a Claude Console organization to your plan. Credits go to that organization each month.
Before you begin, you need:
On your Claude plan:
Max: be the subscriber. Team: be a Primary Owner or Owner
In the Console organization:
the Owner, Admin, or Billing role. If you don't have a Console organization yet, you can create one during the claim flow or at
platform.claude.com
.
To claim your credit:
On claude.ai, go to
Settings > Billing
as a Max subscriber or
Organization settings > Billing
as a Team Owner or Primary Owner.
In the
API credits
section, select "Link organization."
Choose the Console organization you want to receive the credits, or create a new one.
Review the
Supplemental Credit Terms
, then Link organization.
Your credits appear in that organization's balance, ready to use.
Important:
You can link only one Console organization, and each Console organization can receive credits from only one plan. You can't change the linked organization yourself, so choose the one you plan to build in. To change it later,
contact support
.
Tip:
Sign in to the Claude Console with the same email you use on claude.ai. If you’re seeing errors during the linking flow, please try again in a few hours.
What the credits cover
The credits work with any available Claude model on the Claude Platform, including:
The Claude API (Messages API and Message Batches API)
The Playground in the Claude Console
Claude Managed Agents
The Claude Agent SDK
The credits don’t apply to:
Interactive Claude Code in the terminal, IDE, desktop, or web
Extra usage in Claude, Claude Code, or Claude Cowork
Claude on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, or Microsoft Foundry
How the credits work
Refreshes each billing cycle.
New credits arrive shortly after your plan payment goes through. On annual plans, credits arrive monthly.
Doesn't roll over.
Unused credits expire at the end of each billing cycle.
Used first.
Your monthly credits are spent before any credits you've purchased.
Shared across the organization.
Everyone with an API key in the linked organization draws from the same balance.
Separate from your plan limits.
The credits don’t change your usage limits in Claude, Claude Code, or Claude Cowork.
Visible in the Console.
All credits appear on the
Billing
page (platform.claude.com/settings/billing) in the Claude Console with their amount and expiry date.
What happens when your credits run out
If the organization has purchased credits or auto-reload,
usage continues and draws from those.
If the organization has no other credits,
API requests stop until your next monthly credits arrive. Usage is never charged to your Claude plan. To keep going, buy credits or turn on auto-reload in the Console.
If your organization is invoiced through Anthropic sales,
usage beyond the credits is billed as usual.
If your plan changes
Cancel, downgrade to an ineligible plan, or refund.
New credits stop. Credits you already have stay usable until they expire.
Upgrade from Max 5x to Max 20x.
You receive prorated credits right away, then $200 each billing cycle after that.
Move from Max to Team.
Your Max link ends. A Team Owner or Primary Owner can claim the team's credits once the Team plan has been active for seven days.
For Team Owners and Primary Owners
One claim for the whole team.
One owner links a Console organization and claims the pooled credit, up to $500 a month.
The pool follows your seat count.
It's calculated from the seats on your plan each time credits are deposited. For example, a team with three Standard seats and two Premium seats receives $260 a month. Adding another Premium seat would increase the next cycle’s credits to $360.
Control who spends it.
Everyone with an API key in the linked organization can use the balance. To limit usage by project or teammate, set
workspace spend limits
in the Console.
Frequently asked questions
Why can't I use the credits for Claude Code?
The credits are for building your own apps and agents on the Claude Platform. They don't cover interactive Claude Code sessions or extra usage after you hit your plan's limits.
Why don't I see the offer yet?
We’re rolling out API credits over a few days so we might not have gotten to you yet. The offer appears after you've been on an eligible plan for seven days. If you're past seven days and still don't see it, check that you're on a Max or Team plan and that you have one of the required roles. If you think you should be eligible but don’t see the API credits,
contact support
.
Is this the same as the Agent SDK credits announced in June?
No. That credit isn't available. API credits cover the Claude API, Claude Managed Agents, and the Claude Agent SDK, and you claim it into a Console organization.
Can I split my credits across multiple organizations?
No. Credits go to a single Console organization.
I'm on a Pro plan. Can I get this credit?
No. The credits are available on Max and Team plans only.
Does this cover
claude -p
?
API credits cover
claude -p
and the Claude Agent SDK when you run them yourself with an API key from your linked Claude Console organization, because that usage is billed as Agent SDK usage. When you're signed in with your Claude plan instead,
claude -p
and Agent SDK usage still draw from your plan's usage limits and don't use your API credits. Runs started by the Claude Code GitHub Action, an IDE extension or the Claude desktop app count as Claude Code usage, so API credits don't cover them, even with
-p
.

Claude Cowork and chat are one Claude
Updated this week
Copy for LLM
We’re introducing a new way to use both Claude Cowork and chat that removes the distinction between the two products: in the new experience, these are merged into a single conversation, so you don’t need to decide which option better suits your task before getting started. Ask Claude for what you need, and it can decide which tool to use. Claude can answer a quick question, and it can also take on more complex work, like research, reports, spreadsheets, and presentations, and hand it back as finished files you can edit. With the new Claude experience, you ask for all of it in the same conversation, with no mode to choose. What you could previously only do in Claude Cowork is available from any conversation.
The new Claude experience is rolling out gradually, starting with Pro and Max plans on web, desktop, and mobile. On Team plans (in beta) and Enterprise plans, it's available where
Chat and Cowork unified
is turned on.
Why you might not have it yet
We're rolling this new experience out in stages, so even accounts on the same plan will see the changes at different times. You don't need to do anything to enable the new experience. If you're on a Pro or Max plan and your message box still shows "Chat" and "Cowork" options, you don't have it yet. Until then, keep using chat and Claude Cowork as you do today, where you can do most of what's in this article. Your chats, tasks, projects, and settings come with you when your account moves over. Once your account has the new experience, you can't switch back to separate "Chat" and "Cowork" options.
What Claude can do
Hand Claude a whole task
Describe the outcome you want, and Claude works through the steps on its own: searching the web, reading your files, running code, and putting the results together. You don't need to break the work into steps or pick a mode first. A quick question still gets a quick answer, and you can have several tasks running at the same time.
Try: "Go through these five interview notes and pull out the top themes, with a quote for each."
Step away while Claude works
More involved tasks keep running in the cloud even if you close your laptop or leave the page. Come back when the task is done, and the result is waiting in the conversation. Tasks that use files or apps on your computer need Claude Desktop open.
Try: "Research the top project management tools for small teams and write up a comparison. I'll check back later."
Get finished files back
Claude can create documents, spreadsheets with working formulas, and presentations you can open in PowerPoint. Download them and use them anywhere, or ask Claude to keep refining them.
Try: "Turn this analysis into a 10-slide deck I can present on Monday."
Create designs, decks, and docs
Claude can build charts, diagrams, and interactive visuals right in the conversation. Learn more in
Custom visuals in chat and Cowork
. On paid plans, you can also ask for a design, deck, or doc for work you'll put in front of others. Claude Design makes on-brand visuals and mockups, Claude Slides makes presentations, and Claude Docs makes living documents you write with Claude and your team (Claude Design, Claude Slides, and Claude Docs are in beta.) Edit the result yourself or tell Claude what to change, then share it by link or export it. Learn more in
What are artifacts and how do I use them?
Try: "Make a one-page visual summary of this launch plan."
Use the apps you've connected
Apps you've connected to Claude (like Google Drive, Gmail, Microsoft 365, or Slack) work while Claude carries out a task, so it can pull what it needs as it goes. Connect apps in
Customize > Connectors
.
Try: "Find last quarter's board deck in my Drive and summarize what changed since."
Work on the web and on your computer
Files and folders:
In Claude Desktop, give Claude access to a folder on your computer so it can read, organize, and create files there.
Browsing:
Claude can open sites, read pages, click, and fill in forms, using the browser built into Claude Desktop or your own Chrome browser through Claude in Chrome. Learn more in
Use the built-in browser in Claude Cowork
.
Computer use:
In beta on Pro and Max plans, Claude can use apps on your computer directly by clicking, typing, and navigating your screen. Learn more in
Let Claude use your computer in Cowork
.
Claude reaches your local files, the built-in browser, and computer use only while Claude Desktop is open, and by default it asks before permanently deleting any files.
Try: "Organize my Downloads folder by file type and date."
Schedule recurring work
Ask Claude to run a task on a schedule, like a summary of your inbox every Monday morning. Scheduled tasks can run in the cloud, so they keep going when your computer is off. Learn more in
Schedule recurring tasks in Claude Cowork
.
Try: "Every weekday at 8 AM, summarize new messages in my team's Slack channels."
Check in from your phone
A task you start at your desk shows up in Claude Mobile too, so you can see how it's going, answer questions from Claude, and redirect the work from anywhere. You can also start a task from your phone, and Claude keeps working in the cloud.
Make Claude your own
Skills:
Teach Claude how you like a task done, and it follows those steps whenever the task comes up. Learn more in
Use skills in Claude
.
Plugins:
Add plugins that bundle skills and connectors for your role. Learn more in
Use plugins in Claude
.
Choose how much Claude checks with you
A permission setting in the message box controls how independently Claude works:
Auto (default on Pro, Max, and Team plans):
Claude keeps working without stopping to ask about each step, and automated safety checks run before it takes an action.
Manual (default on Enterprise plans):
Claude asks before it takes actions, and you choose whether to allow each one.
You can change the setting at any time, and you can stop or redirect Claude while it works. The setting applies to the whole conversation. For work with real consequences, like sending messages or changing important files, stay close and review what Claude does. Learn more in
Use Claude Cowork safely
.
Pick up where you left off
One conversation list:
Your quick questions and longer tasks live together in
Recents
.
Memory:
Claude uses what it remembers from your chats in the tasks it works on for you.
Projects:
Keep files, instructions, and context together for related work. Projects work in every conversation.
Instructions for Claude:
Set preferences that apply to every conversation in
Settings > Your Claude
(or
Settings > Account
in the older Settings layout).
What happened to Claude Cowork?
In the new experience, everything Claude Cowork does is available from any conversation. Your existing Cowork tasks, projects, connectors, skills, artifacts, and files carry over, and those Cowork tasks open as they did before, so you can continue them. The model picker and the “Code” tab are where they were.
What's in a new place
Cowork tasks:
Together with your chats in
Recents
.
Global instructions:
The Cowork
Global instructions
setting is now part of
Instructions for Claude
in
Settings > Your Claude
(or
Settings > Account
in the older Settings layout). Check that your instructions are what you want.
Web search:
There's no web search toggle. Claude searches the web when it helps.
Research:
Type /deep-research, or click the “+” button below the chat input, then choose “Research.”
Files:
Files Claude creates appear alongside the conversation. In Claude Desktop, the folder Cowork saved its work to is still there. Look for
Storage folder
in
Settings
. Folders you gave Cowork access to are listed under
Trusted folders
.
Memory from local tasks:
Memory from Cowork tasks that ran only on your computer stays with those tasks.
Current limitations
Add from GitHub
isn't supported.
Branching a conversation
from an earlier point isn't available.
Incognito chats
still work, but they open in the previous experience, so Claude can't create files or run code in them.
Search
doesn't include older Cowork tasks. It covers your chats and new conversations, and you can still find older tasks by name in
Recents
.
Dispatch
isn't available to new users. If you already use Dispatch, you can keep using it for now. Learn more in
Assign tasks from anywhere in Claude Cowork
.
How usage works
Everything you do with Claude counts toward your plan's usage limits.  Longer agentic tasks that search the web, run code, or create files generally use more than a quick question. While the new experience rolls out, usage may be measured slightly differently for accounts that have it and accounts that don’t. Check your current usage in
Settings > Usage
, and learn more in
Usage limit best practices
.
Get started
Open Claude and describe what you need, the way you'd brief a colleague. You'll get better results when you include:
Your desired outcome:
what you want to end up with, like "a one-page summary" or "a spreadsheet with a tab for each region."
The format:
how you want the result delivered, like a Word document, a slide deck, or a message you can paste into Slack.
Inputs Claude will need:
the files, links, or apps Claude should work from.
Not sure where to start? Ask Claude what it can help with.

AI-Generated Summary
NVIDIA Minerva
unifies telemetry across GPUs, networking, storage, and workloads into a dynamic knowledge graph that maps infrastructure to active jobs in real time.
Purpose-built supervised and unsupervised machine learning models detect gray failures such as a single NVLink interface degrading among 400,000 or a GPU running hotter than its peers under identical load.
Topology-aware correlation collapses event storms into single incidents; in one case 81 separate alerts from a pause-frame storm were grouped into one actionable incident, cutting repair time and saving an estimated 54 hours of cluster uptime.
An AI agent named Sherlock and an MCP server let operators query live evidence in natural language and integrate operational context into external agentic workflows.
Proactive detection of a rare SuperNIC PCIe fault and an NVMe power-state failure prevented hundreds to thousands of wasted GPU hours by draining affected nodes before customer workloads landed on them.

AI Factories are some of the most technologically complex operational environments ever created. Hundreds of thousands of GPUs, NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet scale-out, scale-across and scale-in fabrics, NVIDIA NVLink scale-up fabrics, distributed schedulers, and multi-week training runs operate in continuous lockstep.These layers function as one production system even when different teams own their telemetry. In synchronous distributed training, a job advances at the pace of its slowest rank. One degraded GPU, interface, storage device, or switch path can waste useful time across many healthy resources.
The failures that hurt yield are often subtle: A GPU runs a few degrees hotter than its peers. An NVMe device loses performance only under sustained load. A switch generates a pause-frame storm that looks like dozens of unrelated symptoms. None of these signals necessarily crosses a static threshold. Together, they create stragglers, extended step times, and delayed checkpoints.
Diagnosis becomes harder because the evidence is split across teams. Network operators see interface counters and fabric events. Compute operators see node and GPU health. ML teams see changing step times, failed jobs, or unstable inference latency. Each view is accurate, but the relationships between them remain hidden. Triage becomes a chain of dashboard searches and cross-team handoffs, which can turn a contained fault into hours or days of lost production time before the affected node or fabric path is identified.
This post covers how NVIDIA Minerva, an AI-native AIOps platform designed around AI factory topology and workloads, addresses these operational gaps.
NVIDIA Minerva collects telemetry across the stack, maps infrastructure to active jobs in a dynamic knowledge graph, applies purpose-built machine learning, and correlates dependent symptoms into high-fidelity incidents. An AI agent-powered assistant and MCP server connected to external agentic tools give operators a conversational path through the same live evidence. The goal is practical: preserve effective GPU hours and keep model training moving.
Why conventional monitoring breaks at AI factory scale
Rule-based monitoring assumes that a known metric crossing a known boundary indicates a known condition. That model works for clear failures. It struggles with so-called “gray failures,” where a component stays available, and the relevant issue may appear only under load or in comparison with peers. Absolute thresholds can miss the shift. Aggressive thresholds often add warnings during normal workload changes, leaving the on-call engineer to decide which deviation matters.
Scale adds alert amplification. One physical fault can produce interface errors, RX (receive) pause frames, congestion indicators, GPU utilization changes, and slower job progress. These observations describe the same dependency chain, but separate dashboards or alerts present them as unrelated events. The on-call engineer receives a  volume of alerts and needs to manually correlate the alerts, determine the signal from the noise, analyze the root cause and the jobs exposed to it.
For operations, the workload is the unit that matters. Teams need to know which job is affected, which resources it occupies, where those resources sit in the physical and logical topology, and how current behavior differs from a healthy baseline. That context must remain current as jobs start and stop and as nodes are drained, replaced, or returned to service. Without it, a healthy component dashboard can coexist with poor job throughput and offer no explanation.
Building a live model of infrastructure and jobs
Figure 1. The NVIDIA Minerva AIOps observability platform
Solving these challenges requires end-to-end visibility across the AI Factory. NVIDIA Minerva ingests metrics, logs, and topology from GPUs, Spectrum-X and NVLink switches, SuperNICs, DPUs, storage, NVIDIA NCCL, schedulers, and AI workloads. Auto-discovery supplies the relationships that raw telemetry lacks. The resulting knowledge graph maps infrastructure, scheduler, and workload elements, then updates those relationships as the environment changes. It can span multiple data centers and support navigation from a factory-wide view to an individual interface.
The topology graph is the key to changing the investigation path. Starting with an anomalous interface, an operator can identify its node, the fabric path it serves, current job placement, and nearby components in the same failure domain. Starting with a job ID, an ML engineer can trace the workload through GPU, host, NIC, switch, and log evidence. Network and compute teams can start from an infrastructure event and see the affected jobs, or conversely see an affected job and investigate the cause using NVIDIA Minerva. Everyone works from the same current causal map instead of reconciling separate inventories.
Detecting gray failures with purpose-built machine learning
NVIDIA Minerva processes billions of metric and log data points per hour with supervised and unsupervised models developed for AI factory infrastructure and workloads. Supervised detection identifies known critical error patterns and can associate recognized conditions with specific remediation guidance. Unsupervised models cover behavior with no predefined signature. They learn normal patterns for a hardware or logical component and compare it with the relevant peers.
Peer comparison matters because a measurement can look acceptable in isolation and still be anomalous in context. Sustained errors on a network interface may look normal in isolation but compared to other interfaces, they stand out as anomalous. A GPU temperature may remain within specification while running substantially hotter than sibling GPUs under the same load. Multivariate models can combine temperature, power, clocks, utilization, and workload state to detect that degradation before the component fails outright.
Logs receive similar treatment. NLP-based anomaly detection surfaces previously unseen patterns, while supervised matching identifies known critical errors. A detection can feed scheduler workflows so an affected node is drained before another job lands on it or at a safe point between checkpoints.
Collapsing event storms into actionable incidents
Figure 2. The NVIDIA Minerva Topology Graph
Topology-aware correlation connects detection to operator action. The correlation engine’s algorithms leverage the knowledge graph to determine which events share a dependency path. Downstream symptoms are then grouped as one incident instead of competing for attention.
The result is less alert noise and more context. NVIDIA Minerva can collapse redundant events and related metric series into a single signal with affected topology and workloads attached. NVIDIA testing shows significant reductions in notified events and tickets for supported scenarios. Operators still need to determine the root-cause using other capabilities provided by NVIDIA Minerva, but they begin with a much smaller search space. Once NVIDIA Minerva creates a high-confidence incident, teams can consume it through the platform UI or existing workflows.
Agentic debugging
Correlated evidence still requires interpretation. NVIDIA Minerva includes a native AI agent called Sherlock which is grounded in live telemetry and the knowledge graph, so an operator can ask why a specific job slowed during a particular interval, which components changed state, or whether other nodes share the same failure domain. Sherlock enables network ops, compute ops and site reliability engineering (SRE) teams to query the system for root-cause-analysis in human language.
Sherlock can present supporting evidence and recommend remediation without requiring every operator to know the exact metric, dashboard, or query language. This gives less experienced operators a route to domain knowledge that has traditionally required escalation to a specialist. Its value in an operations workflow depends on the evidence that Sherlock provides. A recommendation leads back to the telemetry and topology that support it.
NVIDIA Minerva’s MCP server lets external agentic tools query the same operational context. Teams can incorporate live AI factory evidence into their own workflows. Mitigation can remain human approved or selected actions can be automated according to local policy and the risk of the action.
Use cases from NVIDIA AI factories
Detecting a single link degradation in a 400K interface AI factory
In a large AI data center running many multi-node training jobs at once, an SRE noticed one job’s step time slowly getting worse. There was no hard failure, no alert and no obvious culprit. Tracking it down by hand would have meant hours of triage across GPUs, NVLink switches, SuperNICs and the network fabric while the job kept burning GPU hours at reduced throughput.
Instead, NVIDIA Minerva’s Full Stack AIOps Debugging took in telemetry from every layer of the workload topology. Anomaly detection found the one NVLink connection out of roughly 400,000 interfaces that was quietly losing bandwidth. It then linked that NVLink switch to the training jobs whose traffic crossed it. Now that the SRE could see in one UI view the failing link, the affected jobs and where both sat in the datacenter hierarchy, they drained and rescheduled the affected nodes, isolated the link for repair, and brought the jobs back to full speed. The team caught the problem before it spread across the cluster, diagnosed it in minutes instead of hours, and kept the fleet’s goodput and token production up.
SuperNIC Proactive Maintenance
Figure 3. Proactive SuperNIC maintenance
A GPU node logged one kernel line: a hardware error reported by the platform’s firmware (APEI, error source 5). It was a PCIe-level fault on the node’s SuperNIC path. The error was rare enough that no static rule or threshold would have caught it, and it came with no job failure or customer complaint.
NVIDIA Minerva’s real-time rare log anomaly detection marked the message as a rare, never-before-seen event. The platform posted an alert to the cluster operations team’s Slack channel. Alongside the alert, NVIDIA Minerva explained what the error meant and laid out step-by-step remediation, starting with the error context and the system logs to check. The on-call engineer confirmed the fault and removed the node from the allocation pool before any customer workload landed on it. This saved hundreds of GPU hours a failing node would have cost in crashed and restarted jobs.
Straggler job due to NVMe power fault
The ops team was trying to explain why several training jobs were running slower than expected. The slowdown pointed to straggler nodes, but not to a cause.
NVIDIA Minerva’s full-stack job RCA dashboard traced the problem to one host whose logs showed an NVMe device failing. The drive hadn’t been able to wake from a low-power state. The node lost access to its storage, which set off a series of I/O write errors that dragged down every job running on it. With the root cause confirmed, the team drained the node and sent the faulty hardware back for RMA. The fix saved an estimated 5,530 hours of job runtime.
Pause-frame storm
A switch issue produced RX pause frames, GPU utilization spikes, and thousands of metric series. The incident surfaced as many as 81 noisy events. Alerts came in from many devices, but none of them explained the slowdown. The cause was a page fault error that had forced a network switch to restart. The restart set off congestion that spread across the fabric, with RX pause frames propagating between switches, repeated link downs, and spikes in GPU temperature and utilization anomalies.
NVIDIA Minerva’s topology-aware correlation linked 81 separate events and anomalies to the affected job and sent them to the team as a single incident. Handling it as one incident instead of 81 cut time to repair and saved about 54 hours of total cluster uptime.
Turning operational gains into useful compute
NVIDIA’s internal testing shows an increase in mean time between interrupts (MTBI) through proactive maintenance, coupled with a decrease in mean time to repair (MTTR)  through automated root-cause analysis, and a significant reduction in alert noise. These translate into an increase in effective GPU hours by minimizing downtime.
Convergence with DSX OS
NVIDIA Minerva is being developed in alignment convergence with NVIDIA DSX OS. It reuses and plans on integrating selected DSX OS health and resilience components such as NVIDIA Attribution. NVIDIA Minerva capabilities beginning with the data collector will become open-source parts of DSX OS. This provides a modular telemetry foundation aligned with NVIDIA reference architectures while keeping observability, analytics, and automation composable.
Bridging the gap
As AI factories grow in scale and complexity, the gap between traditional monitoring and operational reality widens. NVIDIA Minerva bridges that gap by unifying telemetry across GPUs, networking, storage, and workloads provides the end-to-end observability to detect subtle degradations that static thresholds miss.
By collapsing noisy event storms into single actionable incidents and enabling agentic debugging through conversational AI, NVIDIA Minerva transforms triage from hours of cross-team handoffs into minutes of guided investigation.

NVIDIA Mission Control 2.5
extends its autonomous recovery engine to Kubernetes-based workloads managed by NVIDIA Run:ai.
The engine operates as a three-layer control loop: the Kubernetes scheduler places workloads, the autonomous job recovery service classifies failures using job context, and the autonomous hardware recovery service isolates and diagnoses faulty infrastructure.
During a hardware fault, the job recovery service restarts or reschedules the workload while the hardware recovery service quarantines the node and runs diagnostics in parallel.
For transient software errors, the job recovery service retries the workload without triggering unnecessary hardware remediation.
The hardware recovery service can also detect degradation early and remove risky nodes from the scheduling pool before a job is disrupted.

Training large-scale AI models on thousands of GPUs is a high-stakes operation where monitoring and automation must be built-in to optimize cluster resiliency and uptime at scale. This concept isn’t new to data center operators who have measured mean-time-to-repair (MTTR) and mean-time-between-failure (MTBF) long before AI factories existed.
Now the stakes are higher. Modern
AI factories
run distributed training jobs across hundreds of nodes for days or weeks, and at this scale the operating model changes: hardware anomalies, software errors, network timeouts, and resource contention must be managed proactively to keep workloads on track. Traditional approaches that rely on manual intervention, static checkpointing, and reactive monitoring simply don’t scale when organizations are running dozens of these concurrent multi-node workloads in shared infrastructure.
This is why software services, like the autonomous recovery engine offered in
NVIDIA Mission Control
, are critical to scaling production AI. Previously, the autonomous recovery engine, which can detect, diagnose, and recover from anomalies across the stack, was limited to high-performance computing (HPC) workloads leveraging
Slurm
. As a part of Mission Control 2.5, this service is now extended to Kubernetes-based workloads managed using
NVIDIA Run:ai
.
This post demonstrates how this latest version of Mission Control brings its integrated resiliency framework to Kubernetes workloads, helping AI factory operations move from reactive operational maintenance to proactive, self-healing infrastructure.
Built-in resiliency services
The vision behind Mission Control’s autonomous recovery engine is simple: AI factories should be self-healing systems where failures are detected instantly, recovery decisions are made intelligently based on workload context and failure type, and jobs resume automatically with minimal disruption or wasted compute.
The goal is to understand what failed, isolate anomalies and tag them for maintenance, and return workloads to productive compute with as little wasted time as possible.
Figure 1. In an AI factory, recovery automation should move nodes out of risky or stranded states and back into productive, schedulable compute as quickly as possible to prevent lost work and missed opportunity costs
There are two services that make up the autonomous recovery engine:
autonomous job recovery
autonomous hardware recovery
Because true self-governing resiliency is best understood as a control loop rather than a single recovery feature, the autonomous recovery engine then works with the workloads scheduler (HPC or Kubernetes) providing an integrated three-layer framework where each component plays a distinct but coordinated role.
For this post, we’ll be focusing on scheduling Kubernetes-based workloads.
Figure 2.  The three components of NVIDIA Mission Control 2.5’s autonomous recovery engine: the Kubernetes scheduler, the autonomous job recovery service, and the autonomous hardware recovery service
The three roles in the loop
Let’s start with the Kubernetes workload placement layer. In Mission Control,
NVIDIA Run:ai
is the Kubernetes default scheduler and included as a part of the software. It manages the Kubernetes-based AI workloads, queues, policies, and schedules the jobs onto available capacity.
The autonomous job recovery service provides the workload-context layer. It watches running jobs, tracks where each job is executing, and uses failure history and job topology to classify what kind of recovery path makes sense. The resource manager integration determines how that guidance becomes a restart, retry, re-queue, or placement action.
The autonomous hardware recovery service is the infrastructure-health layer. It monitors nodes and GPUs, removes anomalies from scheduling when needed, and runs diagnostics or remediation so hardware problems do not keep spreading into new jobs.
Keeping these responsibilities separate is what makes the model portable. The autonomous job recovery service doesn’t need to repair hardware and the hardware recovery service doesn’t need to understand every training framework. Finally, the scheduler can steer workloads toward ready capacity without waiting for a root-cause diagnosis.
Failure paths in action
The following scenarios show how the control loop behaves differently in Mission Control depending on the failure signal detected by its autonomous recovery engine.
Scenario 1. Hardware fault during training
A distributed training job is running across a pool of GPUs when one GPU starts to fail. The symptom may appear first as ECC errors, a hung worker, or a communication timeout in the job.
The important thing is what happens next: recovery splits into two parallel tracks. The autonomous job recovery service captures the job context and identifies the suspect node or GPU. The Kubernetes scheduler integration then moves workload recovery forward either by restarting or rescheduling the job.
Figure 3. When a hardware anomaly occurs during a training run, NVIDIA Mission Control is able to restart the job on other healthy nodes while hardware remediation continues
At the same time, the autonomous hardware recovery service isolates the problematic node, records the reason, and starts diagnostics. That hardware path can continue even after the workload is already moving again.
Figure 4. The autonomous hardware recovery service in NVIDIA Mission Control makes the node unschedulable and auditable. Polling then locks triage and starts diagnostics
The value of this path is reduced downtime. The workload doesn’t wait for root-cause analysis before recovery begins, and the faulty node is not accidentally handed to the next job.
Scenario 2. Transient software fault
Not every job failure should trigger hardware remediation. A training worker might exit, hit a recoverable timeout, or lose coordination for a moment even though the underlying node is healthy.
In this path, the autonomous job recovery service uses job context to avoid overreaction. If the failure history looks transient, the system retries according to scheduler policy instead of quarantining hardware that doesn’t need repair.
While NVIDIA Run:ai may express that recovery differently from how it is handled for Slurm, the intent is the same: return the workload to productive execution without unnecessary hardware remediation. The autonomous hardware recovery service keeps monitoring in the background, but it stays out of the recovery path unless new evidence points to hardware.
Figure 5. NVIDIA Mission Control takes into consideration that some job failures are software errors and do not need hardware remediation. In this case, retryable software failures restart automatically and repeated failures are surfaced
The value of this path is restraint. The system restores the workload without creating unnecessary operator noise or shrinking the scheduling pool.
Scenario 3. Hardware degradation caught early
The autonomous hardware recovery service in Mission Control can also detect infrastructure degradation before it becomes a job failure. A node may start showing repeated GPU health warnings, connectivity problems, or other signals that make it risky for future scheduling.
In this path, the autonomous hardware recovery service can remove the node from scheduler eligibility proactively and start diagnostics before an AI training job lands there. The autonomous job recovery service may never need to respond, because the faulty capacity is removed from circulation before it disrupts a workload.
Figure 6. With NVIDIA Mission Control’s autonomous hardware recovery service, suspect hardware is kept out of the scheduling pool while diagnostics and remediation run
In this case, Mission Control’s Kubernetes-based scheduler benefits from a cleaner pool of usable resources. It can avoid placing Kubernetes workloads on suspect capacity similarly to how Mission Control has enabled Slurm to keep faulty nodes out of allocations until they are validated again.
The value of this path is prevention. The system reduces the chance that a known-risk node becomes tomorrow’s AI training outage.
Operational impact
The extension of Mission Control’s autonomous recovery engine to NVIDIA Run:ai marks another step towards achieving a self-healing AI factory. This structure changes resiliency from a scheduler-specific incident workflow into a scheduler-aware operating model.
For platform teams, Mission Control 2.5 delivers a consistent recovery model across both of their Kubernetes and Slurm estates. Faulty nodes are isolated, annotated or recorded, diagnosed, and returned to service only when they are ready.
For AI practitioners, now both Slurm and Kubernetes users can benefit from simpler recovery. Jobs can restart, retry, or requeue according to the scheduler they already use, while the autonomous recovery engine provides the context needed to avoid repeated failures on infrastructure that needs to be serviced.
For the business, the benefit is better utilization of valuable accelerator capacity. The system spends less time stalled in ambiguity and more time keeping training workloads productive.
Video 1. NVIDIA Mission Control demo of autonomous resilience for Kubernetes-based workloads
Get started with Mission Control 2.5

This procedure covers upgrading from Apigee hybrid
version 1.14.x to Apigee hybrid version 1.15.9 and

Use the same procedures for minor version upgrades (for example version 1.14
to 1.15) and for patch release upgrades (for example

If you are upgrading from Apigee hybrid version 1.13 or older, you must first upgrade to
hybrid version 1.14 before upgrading to version 1.15.9.

Changes from Apigee hybrid v1.14
Please note the following changes:
Apigee hybrid monetization

version 1.15.1

supported in Apigee proxy basepaths. To implement this change follow the procedure in

In the most cases, existing policies will continue to function as expected without any issues. However, there is a possibility that policies relying on third-party libraries, or those with custom code that indirectly triggers operations requiring elevated permissions, could be affected.

Before you upgrade to 1.15.9 - limitations and important notes
Apigee hybrid 1.15.9 introduces a new enhanced per-environment
proxy limit that lets you deploy more proxies and shared flows in a single
environment.  See
Limits: API Proxies
to understand the limits on the number of proxies and shared flows you may deploy per
environment.  This feature is available only on newly created hybrid organizations,
and cannot be applied to upgraded orgs. To use this feature, perform a fresh
installation of hybrid 1.15.9, and create a new organization.
This feature is available exclusively as part of the
2024 subscription plan
,
and is subject to the entitlements granted under that subscription. See

to learn more about this feature.
Upgrading to Apigee hybrid version 1.15 may require
downtime.
When upgrading the Apigee controller to version 1.15.9, all Apigee
deployments undergo a rolling restart. To minimize downtime in production hybrid environments

different region/data center). Divert all production traffic to a single cluster and take the
cluster you are about to upgrade offline, and then proceed with the upgrade process. Repeat
the process for each cluster.
Apigee recommends that once you begin the upgrade, you should upgrade all clusters as soon as possible to reduce the chances
of production impact. There is no time limit on when all remaining clusters must be upgraded

Management plane changes do not need to be fully suspended during an upgrade.

Preview, edit, and collaborate on markdown (.md) files natively in Google Docs and Drive
- Google Developers Blog
Preview, edit, and collaborate on markdown (.md) files natively in Google Docs and Drive
OCT. 26, 2026
Sophia Siao
Product Manager
Chelsea Rice
Senior Product Manager
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
Google Workspace is bridging the gap between code and collaboration by providing a familiar, real-time environment where developers and AI agents can seamlessly work together on documentation.
Markdown (.md) is a standard text format widely used by LLMs to preserve structured content—such as tables, headers, and bulleted lists—without the overhead of bulky file formats. Markdown file usage in Google Drive has surged year-over-year, indicating how critical this format has become for modern, fast-paced workflows.
Now, you can natively view, edit, and collaborate in markdown files directly in Google Docs, eliminating the friction of manual file conversions. You can edit without changing file types while ensuring your underlying documentation is preserved for developer tools and git repositories. Plus, with rendered previews in Google Drive, you can easily review formatting with a click.
Built for human and agent collaboration
As AI agents take on larger roles in drafting, planning, and coding, markdown serves as a collaborative common language between humans and AI tools because it is easily readable by both. Google Docs provides a familiar, easy-to-use environment, acting as a shared bridge where team members and autonomous agents work together directly on the same documents. When you open a markdown file in Google Docs, you have:
Native file fidelity:
Manage and edit .md files directly in Google Docs without converting them into a different format. A visible .md badge in the document header clearly indicates you are working in a native markdown file.
Real-time collaboration:
Teammates and AI agents can co-edit the same file to maintain a single source of truth across engineering, product, and AI tools. You can also leverage Google Docs commenting to leave real-time, line-level feedback and track suggestions.
Tracked version history:
Maintain a complete, transparent audit trail of all revisions made across both human contributors and AI agents.
Storage in Drive:
Preview rich, formatted markdown files directly inside Drive—with full support for tables and hyperlinks—or seamlessly toggle to raw text without needing a separate viewer.
Link to Youtube Video
(visible only when JS is disabled)
By combining the simplicity of markdown with the powerful real-time collaboration of Google Docs, teams now have a unified workspace to draft, review, and ship technical content faster.
Availability
Anyone with a Google or Workspace account can get started today by uploading an .md file to Google Drive and begin collaborating directly in Google Docs.

items.title: Streaming comes to API Gateway: real-time and AI-ready APIs, without changing your spec API Gateway now supports real-time streaming—including Server-Sent Events, WebSockets, gRPC,
items.content:
Streaming comes to API Gateway: real-time and AI-ready APIs, without changing your spec
- Google Developers Blog
Streaming comes to API Gateway: real-time and AI-ready APIs, without changing your spec
OCT. 22, 2026
Mak Ahmad
Product Manager
Geir Sjurseth
Product Manager
Jeremy Whitlock
Software Engineer
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
For most of the last decade, an API call looked like a transaction. A client sent a request, waited, and got a complete response back in one piece. That model is exactly what most API management tooling — including API Gateway — was built to handle, and it still describes a huge amount of production traffic.
But that no longer describes all traffic types. A model generating a response emits tokens as it produces them, not in one batch at the end. An agent working through a multi-step task reports progress as it goes. A dashboard, a collaborative editor, a live inference endpoint — these all need a connection that stays open and carries data in both directions.
Until now, developers building those experiences in API Gateway had to make an uncomfortable choice: put API Gateway in front of their APIs and give up streaming, or route streaming endpoints around the gateway and give up the authentication, API key enforcement, and observability that made the gateway essential in the first place. Teams ended up with a split estate — governed APIs on one path, ungoverned streaming traffic on another.
We're announcing that streaming support in API Gateway is available in Public Preview.
Your streaming endpoints can now sit behind the same gateway, with the same policies, as everything else you serve.
For AI applications, streaming also strengthens API Gateway's connection to Gemini platform. A gateway that uses model routing now streams responses from Gemini, Claude and OpenAI gpt-oss models in model garden in Gemini platform as they're generated, and streaming backends you host anywhere else work the same way. Alongside Apigee and Agent Gateway in Gemini platform, API Gateway is the lightweight entry point to Google Cloud's AI gateway capabilities.
What you can stream
API Gateway now supports the full range of streaming patterns modern APIs rely on:
Server-Sent Events (SSE)
— the de facto standard for streaming model output to a browser or client SDK, and the transport behind most OpenAI-compatible chat completion APIs.
Chunked transfer encoding and HTTP response streaming
— including newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON) and any other progressively-delivered response body. Responses are passed through as your backend produces them rather than buffered and delivered at the end.
WebSockets
— full-duplex connections for chat, collaboration, live dashboards, notifications, and interactive sessions.
gRPC streaming
— server-side streaming and bidirectional streaming, so you can put a gateway in front of gRPC services that were previously impossible to proxy.
Streams can stay open for up to one hour. As with any long-lived connection, clients should implement reconnection logic so that a session survives the end of a stream — a well-behaved WebSocket or SSE client should be doing this anyway.
Your API contract doesn't change
This is the part we are most pleased with:
there is nothing new to learn.
Streaming is not a different product, a different resource type, or a different way of describing your API. There are no new extensions to add, no streaming-specific annotations, no separate spec for streaming operations. The same document that describes your existing API describes your streaming API.
Everything you already rely on continues to work exactly as before:
API key enforcement
JWT validation, including Firebase, Auth0, Okta, and Google ID tokens
Service account authentication to backends
Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring integration
Path templating and request routing
During Public Preview, you opt-in when creating the gateway:
gcloud api-gateway gateways create GATEWAY_ID \
--api=API_ID \
--api-config=CONFIG_ID \
--location=REGION \
--enable-streaming
Plain text
Copied
That single flag is the entire difference. At GA, it is planned that streaming will simply be how API Gateway behaves, with no opt-in required and, as during Preview, no changes to your API config.
A hostname you can predict
Alongside streaming, gateways get a deterministic default hostname:
GATEWAY_ID-PROJECT_NUMBER.REGION.gateway.dev
(Example: streaming-test-12345.us-central1.gateway.dev)
Plain text
Copied
Previously the default
gateway.dev
hostname included a generated hash, which meant you could not know your gateway's URL until after you had created it. That is a small thing that causes a lot of friction: you can't write the endpoint into a client config, a Terraform module, a CI pipeline, a firewall allowlist, or a partner integration doc until the resource exists — and if you tear the environment down and rebuild it, the URL changes underneath you.
Now the hostname is a pure function of values you already chose. You can generate it, template it, document it, and commit it to source control before the gateway exists, and you get the same URL every time you rebuild the same gateway in the same project and region. For anyone managing environments as code, or promoting a configuration from dev to staging to prod, this removes an entire category of bootstrapping problem.
Why this matters for AI workloads
Streaming isn't a niche feature for AI applications — it's the expected interaction pattern.
Users expect to see a model's response appear as it's generated, not after a thirty-second pause. Agents need to report intermediate steps. Tool-calling protocols and remote MCP servers depend on long-lived, incrementally-delivered connections. An API management layer that can't stream severely limits the user experience of AI applications.
With streaming, API Gateway becomes a viable front door for that agentic traffic — and the value of a front door is exactly the same as it's always been, only more urgent. AI endpoints are expensive, they consume quota, they need per-consumer authentication and rate limiting, and they need to be observable. These are the governance problems that an AI gateway is intended to solve. The alternative — every team standing up its own proxy in front of its own model endpoint — is how organizations end up unable to answer basic questions about who is calling what.
Model routing
in API Gateway lets you expose a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint and dispatch requests to Gemini, Claude, or OpenAI gpt-oss models based on the model field in the request payload. Model routing plus streaming means clients get a familiar, standards-based streaming interface, while you retain centralized control over which models are reachable, by whom, and under what policy.
Streaming, model routing and
MCP support
are all features within API Gateway that provide a lightweight on-ramp to AI gateway capabilities within Google Cloud. These AI gateway capabilities allow teams to monitor, secure and control agentic traffic of tools, models and agents in their ecosystem, and they're delivered as a composable suite so you can choose the right gateway for each use case. For more expansive AI policies and full lifecycle management, use
Apigee
. To manage and secure agent connectivity, use
Agent Gateway
in Gemini platform. You can also combine these gateways: API Gateway or Apigee can sit in front of your agents and APIs, or behind Agent Gateway so your agents can reach models, tools, and MCP servers. For example, you can route your agent's egress through Agent Gateway for strict security governance, and then pass the request to API Gateway to handle model routing.
What to know during Public Preview
A few things to plan around while the feature is in Preview:
Streaming is enabled at gateway creation time.
Existing gateways can't be converted in place; create a new gateway with the flag to try it.
A few API Gateway features are not available at the initial Preview launch, but will be coming during the Preview time period.
Custom domains via Serverless NEGs and an external Application Load Balancer
Streaming enablement via the Cloud console
Terraform
Latency metrics reflect stream duration.
Request latency for a streaming connection measures the life of the stream, not time-to-first-byte, so expect long-lived connections to change the shape of your latency graphs.
Get started
If you're already using API Gateway, the fastest way to see this working is to point a new streaming-enabled gateway at an existing backend that emits SSE and watch the events arrive incrementally. No spec changes needed.

Architecting Governed, Self-Evolving AI Agents on Google Cloud
- Google Developers Blog
Architecting Governed, Self-Evolving AI Agents on Google Cloud
OCT. 22, 2026
Anant Nawalgaria
Group Product Manager & AI Engineer
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
The Emergence of Self-Evolving AI
As enterprise cloud platforms scale to serve millions of concurrent users, tightly coupled microservices introduce cascading failure modes that no static runbook or threshold alert can anticipate. During high-velocity events like a Black Friday flash sale, Site Reliability Engineers (SREs) face an unforgiving reality: diagnose noisy distributed telemetry in seconds, or suffer cascading outages costing millions of dollars per minute.
While generative AI copilots have accelerated code authoring and log summarization,
AI agents struggle to reliably remediate live production outages
. An on-call engineer battling connection pool starvation does not need an AI agent offering troubleshooting tips or unverified pull requests that might not fix the root cause; they need a governed,
self-evolving AI system
that can:
Diagnose
distributed root causes across cache and database tiers in real time,
Self-patch
by synthesizing, verifying, and mounting executable mitigation tools into live server middleware on the fly,
Self-critique
by computing the marginal credit of every action to separate effective fixes from harmful reflexes,
Remember
by distilling cryptographically signed operational invariants into semantic memory to reduce the chance of identical failures recurring, and
Re-architect
by dynamically rewiring its own multi-agent hierarchy in memory with human sign-off to absorb future surges.
This paradigm is
Self-Evolving AI.
In this Google Cloud research reference architecture, codenamed
Project Chrysalis
, we demonstrate how three foundational research breakthroughs combine into a unified, production-grade architecture that can run on Gemini platform and the Agent Development Kit (ADK). Across simulated Black Friday cache-stampede outages, this governed architecture cut time-to-first-mitigation from 15 to 45 minutes down to 1.8 seconds, reduced HTTP 5xx error rates from 72.7% to 80.0% down to 0.0%, dropped P99 latency from 519.8 ms to 18.2 ms, and evaluated 400 counterfactual traffic policies in BigQuery in ~0.5 ms.
Crucially, this self-evolving architecture does not operate as an unconstrained "black box". To ensure the agent remains secure, reliable, aligned, and contained against rogue behavior, every autonomous action is cryptographically bounded by Google Cloud's defense-in-depth security stack:
Model Armor
to sanitize incoming telemetry against prompt injections and data leaks;
Google Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS)
and Binary Authorization middleware to cryptographically sign synthesized patches and block unverified code from mounting; Open Policy Agent (OPA) Policy Controller to enforce strict SLA guardrails that prevent self-inflicted outages; and Dual-Custody Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) governance to require explicit SRE sign-off before any permanent changes are made to the agent hierarchy.
1. The Incident: The Black Friday Cache Stampede & Why Agents Must Self-Evolve
To see why static playbooks and advisory copilots fail under pressure, consider a classic distributed failure cascade:
The Ingress Surge:
A flash promotion drives a sudden burst of concurrent checkout requests across cold inventory keys.
The Cache Eviction:
Google Cloud Memorystore
(Redis) evicts cold keys under strict Least Recently Used (LRU) memory limits, collapsing the cache hit ratio to zero.
Connection Pool Starvation:
Uncached traffic cascades directly into
Google Cloud SQL
. Once the PostgreSQL connection pool saturates, incoming queries queue past timeout thresholds and the service begins failing with widespread HTTP 500 errors.
The Fatal "3:00 AM Panic Reflex":
Under operational stress, both human responders and naive LLMs instinctively try to
restart the database connection pool
. In a live stampede, dropping connections locks the database kernel, spikes tail latency nearly tenfold, and drives error rates toward total outage.
How a Self-Evolving Agent Adapts Over Time
Conventional AI agents are frozen at deployment with fixed system prompts and pre-registered tools. When a novel infrastructure bottleneck strikes, a self-evolving AI architecture extends those baseline capabilities by synthesizing situation-specific mitigation tools at runtime, scoring the telemetry impact of every intervention, and codifying verified guardrails for future incidents.
For true autonomous resilience,
the agent itself must evolve based on empirical evidence of what worked and what failed
:
Autonomous Self-Patching (Tool Synthesis):
When the agent diagnoses that database starvation is driven by an unthrottled ingress surge and realizes it lacks a built-in traffic-shaping tool, it
writes its own middleware patch
on the fly (an in-memory token-bucket rate limiter), validates its Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), signs it with Cloud KMS, and hot-mounts it directly into the API Gateway.
Causal Self-Critique (Evaluating What Worked vs. What Failed):
After stabilizing the outage, the agent evaluates the telemetry delta of every action taken during the incident. It mathematically penalizes the database restart reflex because it worsened latency, while rewarding its synthesized rate limiter for eliminating server errors.
Cognitive Memory & Organizational Self-Rewiring:
To reduce the likelihood of a repeat outage, the agent writes a signed operational principle into vector memory that blocks database restarts during cache stampedes. It then modifies
its own multi-agent topology in RAM
, commissioning a permanent
Traffic Shaping Specialist Agent
under the supervisor agent so future surges are shaped before they reach the database.
2. The Three Research Pillars of Self-Evolving AI
Self-evolving cloud agents are an active area of applied research focused on resolving the
SRE Trilemma
(balancing exploration safety, structural adaptability, and multi-step credit assignment) by unifying three research pillars on Google Cloud:
1.Serverless Counterfactual Simulation (
Dream-RSI
):
Challenge:
Testing unvetted rate-limiting parameters in live production risks throttling legitimate revenue or re-triggering outages.
Mechanism:
Production request traces are exported to
Google BigQuery
, where the engine replays hundreds of candidate token-bucket configurations in sub-millisecond vectorized memory sweeps to identify Pareto-optimal policies offline.
2. Tri-Level Co-Evolution (
APEX
):
Challenge:
Single-layer prompt tuning provides fragile band-aids, while unconstrained code self-modification risks system instability.
Mechanism:
Agent evolution is separated into three governed timescales:
Layer 1 (Ephemeral Hotpatching):
Synthesizes and mounts in-memory middleware tools to halt active outages in seconds.
Layer 2 (Principle Distillation):
Encodes
Cloud KMS
-signed lessons into
Agent Platform Vector Search
so contraindicated actions are blocked on future alerts.
Layer 3 (Topology Rewiring):
Commissions permanent specialist sub-agents into the active multi-agent Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).
3. Step-Level Shapley Attribution (
AgentEvolver
):
Challenge:
During chaotic incidents, multiple interventions occur in sequence; coarse outcome rewards cannot isolate which step healed the service and which caused collateral damage.
Mechanism:
AgentEvolver computes marginal Shapley credit across each execution span using pre- and post-intervention telemetry deltas (P99 latency, HTTP 5xx rate, and database pool saturation), isolating beneficial patches from erroneous ones.
3. The 4-Phase Reference Walkthrough: Self-Evolution in Action
We
implemented this architecture
as an interactive application on Gemini platform. The diagram above illustrates the closed-loop workflow across the
Production Target Service
,
Agent Development Kit (ADK) Multi-Agent Plane
,
Self-Evolution Engine
, and
Defense-in-Depth Governance Pipeline
.
Each phase of the interactive demonstration showcases a distinct stage of the agent's self-evolution:
Phase 1: Ingress Outage & SRE Baseline
What Happens:
Following a 5-request warm baseline, a 50-request concurrent flash-sale surge hits 15 cold inventory keys.
System Impact:
Memorystore hit ratio drops from
100% to 0.0%
, the Cloud SQL connection pool hits
100% saturation
(2/2 active connections locked), P99 latency spikes to
312.8 to 519.8 ms
, and HTTP 500 errors jump to
72.7% to 80.0%
(40 failed checkouts).
Phase 2: ADK Fast-Loop Triage & Governed APEX Layer 1 Hotpatch
What Happens:
Telemetry alerts wake the
Agent Development Kit (ADK)
Supervisor Router Agent
powered by
Gemini 4 Argon
, after
Model Armor
inspects the incoming alert payload to block prompt injections.
Autonomous Self-Patching:
Diagnosing pool exhaustion, the
APEX Layer 1 Hotpatch Synthesizer
generates an in-memory token-bucket rate limiter (10-token capacity, 40.0 req/s replenishment). Before mounting into the API Gateway middleware, the patch passes three automated governance gates:
AST Sandbox Visitor
verifies that forbidden system modules and dynamic execution sinks are absent.
OPA Policy Controller
confirms the replenishment rate meets the enterprise minimum SLA (>= 10.0 req/s).
Cloud KMS & Binary Authorization
signs the artifact digest (EC_SIGN_P256_SHA256) and verifies key provenance at the middleware boundary.
System Impact:
Across a second 50-request surge,
HTTP 500 errors drop to 0.0%
,
Cloud SQL pool saturation drops from 100% to 0%
,
P99 latency recovers to 18.2 ms
, and excess burst traffic is cleanly shed via HTTP 429 (40 requests throttled, 10 served from warm cache).
Phase 3: AgentEvolver Attribution & Tier-2 HITL In-Memory Topology Rewiring
What Happens:
The
AgentEvolver Credit Attribution Engine
audits the incident execution spans, penalizing the database restart reflex ( after spiking latency to 3,800 ms) and rewarding the token-bucket middleware patch (
+0.97 credit
).
Principle Distillation:
The
APEX Layer 2 Principle Distiller
signs and indexes an immutable operational rule into
Gemini Platform Vector Search
:
"Cache eviction stampede: database restart contraindicated; apply token-bucket load shedding."
Tier-2 Dual-Custody Approval:
Rather than relying on temporary hotpatches, the system proposes a Tier-2 structural update: commissioning a permanent
Traffic Shaping Specialist Agent
. Execution pauses in the UI and presents a
Dual-Custody SRE Approval Modal
requiring explicit sign-off from the on-call SRE.
In-Memory ADK Graph Rewiring:
In production cloud runtimes (Google Kubernetes Engine, Cloud Run), container images are immutable; rewriting source files on disk during a live outage violates container integrity and requires disruptive restarts. Instead, once issued a cryptographic human-approval token, the
APEX Layer 3 Cloud Topology Adapter
executes an
in-memory Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) update:
Instantiates the
Traffic Shaping Specialist Agent
in RAM with dedicated rate-limiting, queue-depth inspection, and token-replenishment tools.
Appends the specialist agent directly to the
Supervisor Router Agent's
active sub-agent graph as a parallel peer alongside the
Diagnostic Agent
(leaving the diagnostic node unmodified).
Updates the supervisor's routing instructions and re-binds the live
Google ADK Runner
in memory with
zero downtime and zero container restarts
.
Phase 4: Google BigQuery Counterfactual Replay & Curiosity Chaos Verification
What Happens:
Incident request traces flow into
Google BigQuery
, where the
BigQuery Counterfactual Replay Engine
executes
400 counterfactual policy simulations
across token capacities and replenishment rates.
Sub-Millisecond Discovery & Chaos Proof:
Vectorized in-memory trace replay completes all
400 sweeps in ~0.5 milliseconds
, identifying the Pareto-optimal policy (5-token capacity, 5.0 req/s rate, zero 5xx errors). Finally, the
Curiosity Chaos Red-Team Agent
stress-tests the evolved system in an isolated shadow sandbox by purging 100% of the cache and firing 200 concurrent requests. The newly wired
Traffic Shaping Specialist Agent
absorbs the surge with
0 HTTP 500 errors
and
13% max DB load
, certifying the architecture as resilient.

Blackstone’s Jas Khaira says fears over AI-buildout debt are overblown
Marina Temkin
3:51 PM PDT · October 21, 2026
Private equity giant Blackstone is putting itself at the center of the AI boom, firm veteran Jas Khaira discussed last week onstage at
TechCrunch Disrupt
.
It is writing checks via various strategies, ranging from offering massive loans to data centers to investing in frontier AI models and applications.
Earlier this year, the firm launched Blackstone N1 (BXN1), a San Francisco-based central hub for its AI initiatives. The group is led by Khaira, who relocated from New York to be at the epicenter of AI.
Unlike earlier tech cycles such as mobile or SaaS, which allowed companies to reach significant scale with moderate capital, the transition to AI requires staggering amounts of investment. That need for capital is precisely why Blackstone, with its $1.3 trillion in assets under management, could play such a critical role in this tech shift.
Khaira emphasized that Blackstone sets itself apart from traditional venture capitalists through its focus on compute financing and its ability to offer flexible capital structures, ranging from debt to equity. And it has been investing aggressively.
“We’re the largest owner of compute outside of the hyperscalers today, whether it’s investments in neo clouds, investments in data centers, and being able to use that compute strategically to support companies,” Khaira said.
For instance, BXN1 played a key role in several compute-related deals, among them
Crux AI,
a neocloud launched in partnership with Google to commercialize its custom TPUs, to which Blackstone committed $5 billion as an investor. It also backed
four-year-old Etched
, a chip startup whose rapid development has caught investor attention. Neoclouds are cloud providers that rent out AI GPU infrastructure.
Blackstone pioneered a financing structure that allowed it to lend massive sums to venture-backed cloud neoclouds by analyzing both committed customer contracts and using GPUs pledged as collateral.
Blackstone’s first such deal came in 2023 with CoreWeave, shortly after that neocloud saw demand explode following the launch of ChatGPT. Despite having only “30 million of revenue and minimal profitability” at that time, according to Khaira, CoreWeave approached Blackstone for a $2.3 billion loan.
CoreWeave was borrowing against the considerable value of its large collection of Nvidia GPUs, with Nvidia also an investor. Blackstone also grew more comfortable with the loan because CoreWeave had contracts with blue-chip customers like Microsoft.
That transaction quickly became the financing model for how Blackstone and other credit institutions provided billions in follow-on debt to CoreWeave and rival neoclouds.
“One of the primary things that we’re looking to is the nature of the customer. And if the customer is an investment-grade customer — let’s say it’s Microsoft or let’s say it’s Meta — the risk gets priced relative to that customer,” Khaira said.
Building on its success with CoreWeave, Blackstone struck other neocloud financing deals, including co-leading alongside Coatue a
$10 billion credit facility
for Australian GPU provider Firmus earlier this year.
Khaira acknowledged that in recent weeks, the large debt burdens accumulated by these companies and other neocloud operators have begun to raise red flags. CoreWeave’s debt alone has since
ballooned to about $50 billion
, for instance.
Khaira said that on the credit side, the market jitters stem from a combination of factors. Interest rates ticked up in September, and hotter-than-expected inflation signals that borrowing costs may keep climbing. The flood of AI infrastructure debt offerings isn’t helping either.
“We’re also seeing higher credit spreads,” Khaira said, explaining that lenders are charging higher premiums on top of already higher base interest rates to finance the AI buildout. “The cost of capital to price in debt for a Meta or a Microsoft has widened out,” he added, pointing out that even tech giants with massive balance sheets and solid earnings are paying more to borrow.
Concerns about the rising cost of debt have spilled into the stock market. Shares of CoreWeave dropped over 20% in recent days, while
Firmus scrapped
its planned IPO on the Australian Securities Exchange at a target valuation of roughly $30 billion.
“Ultimately, the market wasn’t there at that valuation, and so I think as a result, that deal didn’t get done,” Khaira said about Firmus’ canceled listing.
“The market is thinking what is the right price for neoclouds, what is the right price for these businesses in this moment when interest rates are moving up,” he said.
Despite those pressures on some infrastructure providers, AI companies simply can’t get enough compute to power their models. Their appetite continues to drive data center buildout.
Khaira downplayed worries of doom-mongers that the massive accumulation of AI infrastructure debt could lead to a widespread credit crisis or, worse, crash the economy altogether. “This doesn’t feel like something where you’ve got 2008 banks that are shaky credits,” he said.
Instead, he pointed out that because the vast majority of data centers are built for hyperscalers, the debt financing them is ultimately backed “by the most creditworthy companies in the world.”
Beyond funding data centers, Blackstone is helping companies adopt AI through a
$1.5 billion joint venture
called “Ode with Anthropic,” formed alongside Anthropic and Hellman & Friedman this year. Ode supplies forward-deployed engineers to help companies adopt AI and integrate it into their operations, starting with Blackstone’s 280 portfolio companies.
When asked if Blackstone-owned companies are seeing tangible gains from AI, Khaira conceded that “there is definitely ROI, but it is uneven.” He described technology adoption as something that could move in a “sawtooth-type pattern,” which, to skeptics, can look like an oversupply of compute before adoption catches up.

misquoted Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner. We apologize for the error.

Summary
Mistral and NVIDIA are collaborating to revolutionize engineering workflows by integrating Mistral’s AI models with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and physics modeling tools, enabling faster simulations and closed-loop AI-driven design. The partnership will introduce public benchmarks and open datasets to standardize evaluations for physics and agentic AI in computer-aided engineering, while leveraging NVIDIA’s Omniverse for 3D simulation and asset creation. Building on their existing work, including the development of Mistral Large 4, the initiative aims to push the boundaries of AI-powered engineering across industries like aerospace, automotive, and semiconductors.
Mistral is collaborating with NVIDIA to develop a new generation of AI-native engineering workflows powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing. Combining
Mistral Large 4
, with Mistral’s data generation, and physics modeling pipelines, accelerated by
NVIDIA CUDA-X
libraries and
NVIDIA Warp
, the initiative aims to accelerate engineering simulation and enable closed-loop workflows that connect simulation, AI model development and engineering design. Mistral and NVIDIA will also work together to integrate Mistral's models with
NVIDIA Omniverse
libraries for GPU-accelerated 3D scene generation and SimReady asset creation.
A central focus of the collaboration is the development of public benchmarks and open datasets for evaluating physics models. These benchmarks will give researchers, developers and industrial teams a shared foundation to compare model accuracy and performance and build and validate automated CAD-to-simulation workflows.
"For too long, the pace of engineering has been set by the pace of simulation. With Mistral's open-weight models and
physics AI
capabilities, combined with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing stack, we’re giving engineers faster simulation cycles, as well as open benchmarks rigorous enough to validate agents on real CAE and EDA work.” Neil Ashton, VP of Computational Engineering, Mistral
Beyond physics AI, Mistral and NVIDIA will also work together to develop dedicated evaluations and benchmarks for agentic AI in computer-aided engineering (CAE) and electronic design automation (EDA) to accelerate the application of
AI for engineering
within aerospace, automotive and semiconductor use-cases. These benchmarks will assess agents’ ability to use engineering tools, complete multistep workflows and produce technically correct results, while measuring execution time and computational cost.
Through this work, Mistral and NVIDIA will help define standards for agentic and physics AI evaluations in engineering, establishing consistent, reproducible methods for assessing capabilities and tracking progress. Powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing, libraries and tools, Mistral will redefine AI for engineering, transforming how engineers design, simulate and build the next generation of products.
“The next wave of engineering breakthroughs will come from exploring ideas that were once too complex or time-consuming to test,” said Tim Costa, vice president and general manager of industrial and computational engineering at NVIDIA. “By combining Mistral’s advanced open models and deep expertise in physics AI with NVIDIA accelerated computing and libraries, we’re helping engineers push the boundaries of design—with shared industry benchmarks to build confidence in what AI can do.”
Building on the ongoing NVIDIA and Mistral partnership
The industrial engineering collaboration builds on an ongoing partnership between NVIDIA and Mistral spanning open model development, domain-specific AI and the infrastructure needed to bring these capabilities into production.
The companies previously co-developed
Mistral NeMo
and are now
working together
through the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition to develop a frontier base model that will continue to advance the open weight frontier.
